title: Memory: from physical cells to processes, NUMA and durable data
industry_title: Memory management, NUMA and persistent data

paras: This chapter deepens earlier chapters on hardware, Linux processes, containers, storage and distributed systems. Original notes are referenced, not yet published in this build; editorial corrections are separate.
Reading path: CPU request → virtual address → page tables / TLB → physical frame → NUMA locality → storage and recoverability.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 1: Memory hierarchy and Linux allocation
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: Pages, process segments, NUMA nodes and physical memory zones describe different concerns. Pages are fixed-size virtual-memory units; frames are physical RAM units. Segments are logical regions such as text, data, heap and stack. NUMA nodes group memory by locality, while zones express allocation constraints. These are not four levels of one hierarchy.
Source: B015/P01 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 2: RAM, page allocator, page structs and tmpfs
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: DRAM stores volatile bytes. Linux tracks physical page frames through struct page metadata (with newer folio abstractions), and allocates them using page allocators such as the buddy allocator. tmpfs is a memory-backed filesystem with possible swap backing, not a general-purpose page allocator. The page cache accelerates file I/O.
Source: B015/P02 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 3: Volatile RAM versus nonvolatile storage
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: RAM holds active working data; NAND flash and NVMe SSDs retain data without power. NVMe is a storage interface/protocol, not a memory technology. Data can be copied between storage and RAM, but a backup must be an independently recoverable copy, not merely a live RAM workspace.
Source: B015/P03 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 4: Backup and recovery paths
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: Backups protect recoverable data and configuration. Tools mentioned include rsync, tar, dd, gzip and zstd; each has a different role. rsync copies/synchronizes files, tar archives, compression tools reduce size, and dd copies raw blocks. Redis persistence and tmpfs are not interchangeable with durable backup systems. Verify restoration, retention and off-site copies.
Source: B015/P04 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

Editorial technical synthesis: Linear addressing, segmentation, paging and segmentation-plus-paging are address translation and organization mechanisms. Modern x86-64 Linux primarily uses paging with a largely flat segmentation model. Virtual addresses are translated via page tables and hardware translation caches (TLBs).
Source: B015/P05 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 6: UMA, NUMA, shared and distributed memory
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: UMA and NUMA describe memory access latency characteristics within shared-memory multiprocessor machines. NUMA memory is shared-address-space but local versus remote accesses may differ in latency. Distributed-memory nodes have separate address spaces and communicate explicitly, usually over a network. SMP and MPP are architecture labels, not mutually exclusive synonyms for UMA and distributed memory.
Source: B015/P06 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

blocks.h2: B015 · Page 7: CPU architecture and locality
paras: Editorial technical synthesis: ISA names such as x86-64, ARM and RISC-V are distinct from memory architecture. Cache-coherence and memory locality affect multicore performance. SIMD and vector units describe instruction/data parallelism; MIMD describes multiple independent instruction streams. NUMA-aware placement can improve performance when workloads and memory remain local.
Source: B015/P07 · original image referenced, not yet published here · interpretations and corrections editorial.

Earlier hardware and chip chapters: DRAM cells, controllers, PCIe and NVMe explain the hardware behind page frames and persistent storage. Linux process chapter: text, data, BSS, heap and stack are virtual-memory mappings of a process. Containers: cgroups account/limit memory; namespaces isolate views but do not create private physical RAM. Kubernetes: scheduler requests and limits are resource policies; Linux enforces memory accounting and OOM behavior on nodes. Networks and distributed systems: a remote NUMA node is not the same as remote RAM across a network; distributed memory requires explicit communication or specialized software.

blocks.h2: Applied path: a web request and memory
paras: NIC receives packet → kernel networking allocates buffers → application process accesses virtual addresses → CPU MMU translates addresses to physical frames → caches and NUMA locality affect latency → database or filesystem writes eventually persist to storage → separate backups enable recovery. These steps are a conceptual path, not a guarantee that every packet follows precisely the same allocation sequence.
